intro: At, on and in show when something happens: at 8 o'clock, on Monday, in June. The choice follows a simple logic, from the most exact (at) to the longest periods (in), with a few fixed expressions to learn.
objectifs: Use at for clock times and exact moments, on for days and dates, in for months, seasons, years and parts of the day.
Remember the exceptions: at night, at the weekend, on Monday morning.
Know when to use no preposition: this, next, last, every, today, tomorrow.
Use from… to, until, before and after for a period or a simple time reference.

texte: Imagine a pyramid: at the top, the most exact time (at + a clock time); in the middle, a day (on); at the bottom, longer periods (in + month, season, year, century).
The type of time decides, not the verb.

lignes: at 7 o'clock, at half past six, at noon, at midnight, at lunchtime, at the moment
at Christmas, at Easter, at the weekend
on Monday, on Fridays, on my birthday, on Christmas Day
in June, in (the) winter, in 2025, in the 21st century
in the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening

exemples: The meeting is at ten o'clock.
We go to the beach in summer.

texte: We say “in the morning / in the afternoon / in the evening”, but “at night”, with no article.
When you say the day, “on” wins: on Monday morning, on Friday evening, on the morning of 3 May.
The weekend: “at the weekend” in British English, “on the weekend” in American English. Holidays: “at Christmas” (the Christmas period), but “on Christmas Day” (25 December).
exemples: What do you do at the weekend?
We visit our family at Christmas.

texte: Don't use at, on or in before this, next, last, every, or before today, tomorrow, yesterday, tonight. Say “next Monday”, not “on next Monday”; “this morning”, not “in this morning”.
This is a very common mistake: “every day”, “next week”, “tonight” need no preposition.

In British writing: on 5 May or on 5th May. In American writing: on May 5 or on May 5th. When you speak, use the ordinal number: “on the fifth of May” (UK) or “on May fifth” (US). Ordinal numbers (first, second, third…) are in lessons 22 and 89.
For a year alone: in 2026 (“in twenty twenty-six”). For a month and a year: in May 2026.
exemples: Say: on the fourteenth of July.
“was born”: learn it as a fixed phrase.

texte: For a period with a start and an end: “from … to …” or “from … until …”: The shop is open from 9 to 6. “Until” (or “till”, more informal) shows the end: I work until five.
“Before” and “after” go before a time or a noun: before lunch, after work, after ten o'clock. For a time in the future, “in” means “after this amount of time”: The bus leaves in ten minutes.
exemples: The bank is open from Monday to Friday.
I'm at the office until six.
The film starts in five minutes.
in + amount of time in the future.

formule: at + clock time / exact moment / night / the weekend · on + day / date · in + month / season / year / the morning · Ø + this / next / last / every / today / tomorrow
prononciation: In the sentence, “at” is weak: /ət/ (at six /ət ˈsɪks/). The time has the stress.
“on” /ɒn/ and “in” /ɪn/ join the next word when it starts with a vowel: on_April, in_August.
Days of the week are stressed on the first syllable: MONday /ˈmʌndeɪ/, WEDnesday /ˈwenzdeɪ/ (the first d is silent), THURSday /ˈθɜːzdeɪ/.
In a spoken date, “the” and “of” are weak: on the fifth of May /ɒn ðə ˈfɪfθ əv ˈmeɪ/.
erreurs: No preposition before next, last, this, every.
The bus leaves after ten minutes. (ten minutes from now)
The bus leaves in ten minutes.

dialogue.contexte: Two colleagues in Brussels plan a meeting with a Canadian client.
lignes: When is the meeting with the Canadian client?
It's on Thursday, at three o'clock our time.
Thursday? I'm at the dentist's in the afternoon. Can we do it in the morning?
in the afternoon / in the morning.
Not really. In Montréal it's six hours earlier, so nine in the morning here is three in the morning for them.
Ha! They don't work at night! What about next Monday?
Monday is fine. They're free from eight to eleven, their time.
Perfect. So on Monday at four, our time. I'm in the office until six.
Great. I'm sending them an email in five minutes.

mots: the early part of the day
the time between 12 pm and the evening
the end of the day, before night
The street is quiet at night.
the time when it is dark and people sleep
What are you doing at the weekend?
the day you were born, every year
The shop is open until eight.

exercices.consigne: Complete with at, on or in.
Complete with at, on, in or Ø (no preposition).
items: We're going to Kribi ___ next week.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: I go to the gym in Mondays.
I go to the gym on Mondays.
The café is open since 7 to 11.
The café is open from 7 to 11.

exercices.consigne: Use the words and add the right preposition (or none).
items: I / get up / six / the morning
I get up at six in the morning.
We don't work at the weekend. (US: on the weekend / on weekends)
My birthday is on 3 March. / My birthday is on the third of March.
it / be / cold / winter / in Canada
It's cold in winter in Canada.

exercices.consigne: Describe your week in five sentences with at, on, in and one expression with no preposition (every, next…).
items: I start work at eight in the morning. On Wednesdays I finish at three. I play football every Saturday. In summer, we often eat outside in the evening. Next month I'm on holiday.

a_retenir: at + clock time, exact moment, night, Christmas, the weekend (UK).
on + day, date, Monday morning, my birthday.
in + month, season, year, century, the morning / afternoon / evening.
No preposition before this, next, last, every, today, tomorrow, tonight.
from… to / until for a period; in + amount of time = after that time from now (in ten minutes).
